title: Indexes & query plans: making the right reads cheap
objectives: Explain what a B-tree index makes cheap (equality, ranges, sorted reads) and what it costs every write
Read `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output — scan types, estimated vs actual rows — and run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a write inside a rolled-back transaction
Order a composite index's columns for a query: equality columns first, then one range or sort column (leftmost prefix, softened by PostgreSQL 18 skip scan)
Use partial and unique indexes, and make a partial unique index the `ON CONFLICT` target by repeating its predicate
Diagnose why an index isn't used: a function or cast on the column, a leading-wildcard or non-C-collation `LIKE`, a condition that matches most rows, stale statistics

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes
PostgreSQL 18 docs: PREPARE (generic vs custom plans)

questions.prompt: An `events` table takes thousands of inserts a second. Someone adds six indexes so every dashboard query is fast. What did that cost?

options.text: Every insert now also writes an entry into each of the six indexes, so inserts get slower and the table's total size grows
Nothing at write time — indexes are only consulted by reads
Reads get slower, because the planner has more indexes to choose between
Each index is rebuilt nightly, which locks the table

questions.explanation: The manual: once an index exists, the system has to keep it synchronized with the table, which adds overhead to data manipulation. An insert touches the table *and* every index on it (every partial index whose predicate the row meets). For a write-heavy table that's the trade to weigh — and the reason to drop indexes nothing uses. Indexes aren't rebuilt on a schedule, and the planner's extra work to consider six more indexes is small next to the write cost.

questions.prompt: To see why a cleanup is slow, you run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now() - interval '30 days'` on production. What happened?

options.text: The rows were deleted — `ANALYZE` executes the statement; only a `SELECT`'s output is discarded
Nothing changed; `EXPLAIN` never executes anything
It ran in an automatic dry-run transaction that was rolled back
It failed: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` only accepts `SELECT`

questions.explanation: Plain `EXPLAIN` only plans. With `ANALYZE` the statement really runs so PostgreSQL can measure it, and the manual is explicit that side effects happen as usual. To measure a write safely: `BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE …; ROLLBACK;`. There is no automatic dry-run.

questions.prompt: A plan node says `(cost=… rows=12 …) (actual time=… rows=48210.00 loops=1)`, right after a nightly bulk import. What's the first thing to do?

options.text: Run `ANALYZE` on the table — the planner is estimating from statistics that predate the import
Add another index on the filtered column
Run `VACUUM FULL` to compact the table
Nothing — estimates are always rough, so a 4,000× miss is normal

questions.explanation: The first numbers are the estimate, the `actual` ones are what happened. A miss that large means the planner chose its plan for 12 rows and got 48,210, so a nested loop or an index scan picked for "a few rows" is now doing far more work. The manual's first rule for examining index use is to run `ANALYZE` so the statistics reflect the data. More indexes or a `VACUUM FULL` don't fix estimates.

questions.prompt: The hot query is `WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at >= $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50`. Which index?

options.text: `(tenant_id, created_at)`
`(created_at, tenant_id)`
Two separate indexes, one on `tenant_id` and one on `created_at`
`(created_at)` alone — the range and the sort are both on it

questions.explanation: Equality columns first, then the range or sort column. `(tenant_id, created_at)` jumps to this tenant's section, where entries are already in `created_at` order: read the newest 50 and stop. `(created_at, tenant_id)` makes the scan walk every tenant's rows in the date range and filter — in the reading's test the same 13 rows cost 523 pages instead of 16. Two single-column indexes can be combined with a bitmap, but that loses the ordering, so the `ORDER BY` needs a sort.

questions.prompt: There's an index on `(customer_id, created_at)` with thousands of customers. A new query filters only on `created_at > now() - interval '1 day'`. What should you expect?

options.text: The index is a poor fit — that day's entries are scattered across every customer's section — so expect a different plan; add an index led by `created_at` if the query matters
It uses the index fully: an index can be searched on any of its columns
PostgreSQL 18 skip scan makes column order irrelevant, so it's as good as an index on `created_at`
The query errors because it doesn't mention the first indexed column

questions.explanation: The index is sorted by `customer_id` first; dates are only ordered within each customer. PostgreSQL 18's skip scan can run one search per leading value, but the manual says it's generally chosen only when there are *few* distinct values — with thousands of customers the whole index would have to be read, so the planner usually prefers a sequential scan. Nothing errors: an unsuitable index simply isn't used.

questions.prompt: `users` has `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE …` fails with `42P10: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification`. Why?

options.text: Inference only picks a partial unique index when the statement repeats its predicate: `ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
`ON CONFLICT` only works with constraints, never with indexes; name it with `ON CONSTRAINT users_email_live`
Another transaction is holding a lock on the index
A soft-deleted row with the same email exists

questions.explanation: The manual: the optional `index_predicate` in the conflict target is what allows inference of partial unique indexes. Without it, PostgreSQL looks for a non-partial unique index on `(email)`, finds none, and raises `42P10`. `ON CONSTRAINT` fails differently — a unique *index* isn't a constraint (`42704 … does not exist`). This is also why PostgREST/supabase-js `onConflict: 'email'` can never target this index: it sends a column list with no `WHERE`.

questions.prompt: 95% of orders have `status = 'shipped'`. There's an index on `status`, yet `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped'` uses a Seq Scan. What's going on?

options.text: The planner is right: fetching 95% of the rows through an index costs more than reading the table straight through
The index is corrupt and needs `REINDEX`
B-tree indexes don't work on `text` columns
The planner never uses an index unless `enable_seqscan` is off

questions.explanation: An index pays off when it's selective. Pulling 190,000 of 200,000 rows via index lookups means visiting nearly every table page anyway, in a worse order. For a skewed column, index the rare values with a partial index (`… WHERE status = 'open'`). `enable_seqscan = off` is a diagnostic for testing, not a setting the planner needs.

questions.prompt: On a database with collation `en_US.UTF-8`, `WHERE email LIKE 'ada%'` does a Seq Scan even though `email` has a plain B-tree index. The fix?

options.text: `CREATE INDEX … ON users (email text_pattern_ops)` — the default operator class can't serve `LIKE` outside the C collation
Rewrite it as `LIKE '%ada%'` so the index can match anywhere
Use a hash index — they're designed for string matching
Nothing can help: `LIKE` never uses an index

questions.explanation: A B-tree can serve a left-anchored `LIKE`, but per the manual, in a database not using the C locale it needs an index with the `text_pattern_ops` operator class, which compares strictly character by character (keep the default index too if you run `<`/`>` range queries). A leading wildcard rules out any B-tree — that needs `pg_trgm`. Hash indexes handle only equality.

prompts.prompt: Index for `WHERE customer_id = $1 AND created_at >= $2 ORDER BY created_at`.
prompts.explanation: The equality column leads, so the scan jumps straight to one customer; within that customer the entries are sorted by `created_at`, so the range is one contiguous slice and the `ORDER BY` needs no sort.

An index on `email` can't answer a question about `lower(email)` — the stored values are different. An expression index stores `lower(email)`, and the planner uses it when the query contains that same expression.

prompts.prompt: Unique email among live users; soft-deleted rows may repeat it.
prompts.code: CREATE ___ INDEX users_email_live ON users (email) ___ deleted_at IS NULL;
prompts.explanation: The `WHERE` clause makes it a partial index: only rows that satisfy the predicate are in it, so uniqueness is enforced among them and nowhere else.

prompts.prompt: Upsert against that partial unique index.
prompts.explanation: The `WHERE` in the conflict target lets inference choose the partial unique index; leave it out and you get `42P10`. `EXCLUDED` is the row that was proposed for insertion, so `EXCLUDED.name` is the incoming value.

prompts.prompt: Measure a delete without keeping its effects.
code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now() - interval '30 days';
prompts.explanation: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the statement. Inside a transaction you then roll back, the plan and timings are real and the rows are untouched — the recipe from the `EXPLAIN` reference page.

code: -- orders: 200,000 rows; status is 'shipped' on 95% of them, 'open' on 5%.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped';
snippets.question: What's the top plan node?
acceptable: seq scan — the index isn't used
snippets.explanation: The planner estimates 190,000 matching rows; reading them through the index would visit nearly every page in random order, so a straight sequential read is cheaper. The same index *would* be used for `status = 'open'` (5%). Low selectivity, not a missing index.

code: CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);   -- 100,000 users
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user42@example.com';
snippets.question: Does the plan use `users_email_idx`?
snippets.explanation: The index stores `email` values, and `lower(email)` is a different value for every mixed-case address, so the index can't locate matches. Either compare the bare column (store emails normalised) or create an expression index on `lower(email)` — which the same query then uses with `Index Cond: (lower(email) = …)`.

code: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
INSERT INTO users (email, name) VALUES ('ada@x.io', 'Ada Lovelace')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name;
snippets.question: What happens when a live `ada@x.io` already exists?
snippets.answer: ERROR 42P10: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification
snippets.explanation: Most people expect an update. But the conflict target `(email)` infers only a *non-partial* unique index on `email`, and there isn't one. Adding `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` after `ON CONFLICT (email)` makes it work. The error happens even when no conflicting row exists — inference fails before any row is checked.
